cells.tense: Right now you can feel which structures simply won't bear their own weight.
cells.act: do the small practice again, alone, today
cells.ask: Find some small practice you've let drop and do it again today, by yourself. No plan for where it leads, no improving it. If it feels like nothing, keep going anyway — the plain repetition is the whole task.
cells.core:
You can feel which structures are truly bearing weight and which are a front. A false thing shows itself to you before it breaks, and you don't have to shove it over — you stop carrying the weight. The working version: your attention goes to what's true nearby, what falls does so without your help, and what remains is real.

The risk is that the falling becomes the event you keep watching, and you're already scanning for the next crack instead of staying with what held. Attention keeps drifting. Pick some small practice and repeat it today, alone, unremarkable, no refinement. Solitude is not withdrawal here; it's the quiet that keeps your read honest.
cells.sheetLine: You feel what won't hold. Let one thing stay.

cells.tense: You will pull things down before they have had a chance to stand at all.
cells.act: join the practice the others keep
cells.ask: Join one practice other people already keep — a class, a standing meetup, a shared routine — and sit through the ordinary part. Do it their way, not your improved way. Go once before you decide anything.
cells.core:
When this tips, everything looks like it might fall, so you take it down early. It feels like clear sight, and how you describe it, the structures deserved it. But you're running ahead of what's here, and those closest to you have quit handing over the things they'd want kept. That's the signal worth trusting. Clearing feels like air to you; from across the table, it comes over as nothing being allowed to settle.

Contact is what's thin, not restraint. Join the practice the others keep, sit through it whole, and hold to the shared part when your own read says pull it down. Staying present with them before the thing is over teaches you what can stay.

cells.tense: Something closed behind you long before now and your arms are still holding it wide.
cells.act: build the smallest structure that holds it
cells.ask: Take the thing you're propping up and put a boundary on it: one date, one rule, one line. Then work only inside that and leave the rest alone. Let the boundary carry it instead of your hands.
cells.core:
You're at a door that shut behind you, holding it wide with both hands. It isn't that you don't see it — you see it. That's the hard part. The same read that spots a false structure across a table has already told you this one is dead, and finite hours are going into propping it up. From outside it looks like steady service; from inside it's a grip that won't loosen.

More insight won't move this. Put a small structure around it — one clear line, one date, one rule — so it no longer needs your hands. Then work only inside that. The frame that quit holding doesn't need your arms under it.
cells.sheetLine: You saw it first. Your arms are still holding it up.

cells.tense: You are already stepping away from the plan you keep calling the plan.
cells.ask: Begin the thing you want before you're ready, today, with no announcement and no revised plan. Let the pull choose the direction and keep the first piece tiny. The explanation can arrive after.
cells.core:
You're acting on what you see, yet you describe it as though it were happening to you. In your telling, the changes arrive from somewhere else; meanwhile a structure is being set down, quietly, by your hand, and the story you tell still has you on the old road. Your read runs further along than the account you give.

What returns this is simpler and earlier than any analysis: start from the pull itself, before you feel ready. Begin the thing you actually want today, not the tidy version that's already been spoken for. Move first, and the reasoning lands behind you, so the departure has its first fact.
cells.sheetLine: You're already moving. The plan hasn't caught up.
